description: Given a plain-language request, the skill should author (or edit) an Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML that matches the request -- including, where asked, an `anomalies` block at the correct level (pipeline/task/operation) with the correct type, threshold, and destinations, per the anomaly detection section of yaml-authoring.md.

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Core dbt Build' that runs our dbt Cloud job (job_id 555111) on a cron trigger, daily at 3am UTC. I want to know if the whole run ever takes noticeably longer than usual -- say 25% longer than normal -- and have that posted to our #data-eng-alerts Slack channel. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a DBT (dbt Cloud) task running the given job on a 3am daily cron, plus a pipeline-level `anomalies` block (type `pipeline_duration_above_baseline`, `percentage_above_baseline: 25`) with a SLACK destination targeting #data-eng-alerts. No task-level or operation-level anomaly block, since only overall pipeline duration was asked about.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
An above-baseline pipeline anomaly type is used
Threshold is set to 25%
Anomaly notifies the requested Slack channel
Uses the DBT integration for the dbt Cloud job
Scheduled daily at 3am UTC
The `anomalies:` block sits at the pipeline's top level (a sibling of `pipeline:`, `schedule:`, `alerts:`), not nested inside a task
Does not add an operation-level (operation_duration_*) anomaly block -- the user only asked about overall pipeline duration, not individual dbt models
Does not add a task-level (task_duration_*) anomaly block in addition to the pipeline-level one -- only the pipeline-level monitor was requested

evals.prompt: Here's our existing pipeline in files/orders_sync_pipeline.yml. The nightly Fivetran sync task 'sync_orders' sometimes finishes way faster than usual, which we've learned means it silently picked up zero new rows. Add anomaly detection to that task so we get flagged when it finishes more than 80% faster than its normal baseline -- no Slack needed for this one, just flag it in the UI is fine. Leave the rest of the pipeline as-is. Write the updated pipeline to pipeline.yml.
evals.expected_output: The same pipeline as the fixture, unchanged, except the `sync_orders` task now has a task-level `anomalies` block: type `task_duration_below_baseline` (explicit, since type is required for below-baseline), `percentage_below_baseline: 80`, no destinations. The `dbt_build` task, schedule, and failure alert are preserved exactly as in the fixture.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
A below-baseline task anomaly type is used
Threshold is set to 80%
The sync_orders task is still present
The unrelated dbt_build task from the fixture is preserved
The existing failure alert from the fixture is preserved
The `anomalies:` block is nested under the sync_orders task specifically, not under dbt_build and not left at the pipeline level
No destinations are added to the anomaly block, matching the user's 'just flag it in the UI' request
The 2am UTC schedule and the FIVETRAN/DBT_CORE task configuration from the fixture are otherwise left unmodified

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Partner Feed' with a single HTTP task that POSTs to /v2/ingest on our partner API. It needs a JSON body of {"mode": "full"} and a custom header X-Partner-Id set to acme. Kill the task if it hasn't finished 45 minutes after it was queued. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with an HTTP / HTTP_REQUEST task whose `body` and `custom_headers` parameters are quoted JSON *strings* rather than bare YAML mappings, plus a `configuration.timeout` of 2700 (45 minutes expressed in seconds) on the task.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the HTTP integration
Uses the HTTP_REQUEST job
Timeout is expressed in seconds, not minutes
`body` is a quoted JSON string, not a nested YAML mapping — the parameter's schema type is string, so a bare mapping is rejected
`custom_headers` is likewise a quoted JSON string carrying X-Partner-Id, not a nested YAML mapping
`timeout` sits under a `configuration:` block (on the task, or at pipeline level), not as a bare task key
Does not set a timeout above 259200 seconds, the schema maximum

evals.prompt: We want an Orchestra pipeline called 'Partner Sync Reaction' that a partner's system triggers by POSTing their own event JSON — it looks like {"connection_id": "abc-123", "event": "sync_completed"} and we can't change its shape. The pipeline should run a Python task, but only when connection_id is abc-123. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with the webhook trigger enabled and pipeline `inputs` that the partner's payload is mapped into via `${{ outputs.payload[...] }}`, with the task gated by a `condition` reading the mapped input as `${{ inputs.<name> }}`.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
The webhook trigger is enabled
Declares pipeline inputs the payload is mapped into
The task is gated by a condition referencing a mapped input
The payload reaches the pipeline through `${{ outputs.payload }}` (whole body or a subscript such as `${{ outputs.payload['connection_id'] }}`) in the webhook trigger's run input mapping
Does not reference `${{ outputs.payload }}` from a task parameter or condition directly — it is only readable in the trigger's run input mapping, and must be mapped to an input first
Does not try to reshape the partner's payload into Orchestra's start-pipeline format, or treat a non-matching body as an error — any JSON body starts the run

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Nightly Transform' with a single AWS Batch task that submits to the analytics-prod job queue using the nightly-transform job definition, pinned to revision 3. Override the container command to `python transform.py` and set STAGE=prod in the container's environment. AWS Batch should kill an attempt that has been running for more than 30 minutes. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with an AWS_BATCH / AWS_BATCH_SUBMIT_JOB task: job_queue analytics-prod, job_definition nightly-transform:3, a `container_overrides` written as a real nested YAML mapping (command list plus an environment list of name/value objects) rather than a quoted JSON string, and `timeout_seconds: 1800` — the per-attempt Batch limit — rather than a `configuration.timeout`, which would only fail the task and leave the job running.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the AWS_BATCH integration
Uses the AWS_BATCH_SUBMIT_JOB job
The job definition is pinned to revision 3
The 30-minute attempt limit is expressed as timeout_seconds: 1800, in seconds
`container_overrides` is a nested YAML mapping, not a quoted JSON string — unlike HTTP `body` or Python `environment_variables`, this parameter's schema type really is an object
The container environment is a list of {name, value} objects (STAGE / prod), not a bare key-value mapping
The attempt limit is set with the task's own `timeout_seconds` rather than only a `configuration.timeout` — a task timeout fails the task without terminating the Batch job
Does not set timeout_seconds below 60, the schema minimum

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Daily Revenue' that first pulls the Snowflake credentials out of our Azure Key Vault and then uses them to run `SELECT * FROM revenue` on Snowflake. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML containing only the SNOWFLAKE / SNOWFLAKE_RUN_QUERY task, with its credentials referenced through `connection:`. No Key Vault task is authored: AZURE_KEY_VAULT is an integration with no integration_job — a credential store a connection reads its own credentials from — so the fetch is configured as Credential Store on the Snowflake connection and the credentials never move through the pipeline. The response says so rather than inventing a job name.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Authors the Snowflake query task
No secret-fetch task is invented — every task in the pipeline is the SNOWFLAKE one
No credential value is written into the YAML

Explains that AZURE_KEY_VAULT has no integration_job and cannot be a task — it is a credential store selected on the Snowflake connection, so the vault lookup happens when Orchestra uses that connection, not as a pipeline step
Does not invent a job name such as AZURE_KEY_VAULT_GET_SECRET, and does not substitute a PYTHON or HTTP task that calls Key Vault itself to work around the missing job
Does not pass the credential between tasks via set_outputs or a parameter reference — there is no secret value in the pipeline to pass

evals.prompt: Add a task to pipeline.yml called 'Summarise Incidents' that runs our Orchestra agent a1b2c3d4-0000-4000-8000-000000000001 with the prompt 'Summarise today's open incidents', and feed its answer into the Slack task that already posts to #data-alerts. Keep the agent on whatever model and effort it is already configured with. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An ORCHESTRA / RUN_AGENT task carrying only agent_id, prompt and set_outputs: true, with model_id, effort, llm_integration and llm_connection_id left out so the task inherits the agent's own settings, and the Slack task referencing the agent task's output rather than being left unwired.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Uses the ORCHESTRA integration for the agent task
Uses the RUN_AGENT job
The agent id given in the request is used verbatim
set_outputs is true on the agent task, since a downstream task reads its answer
model_id and effort are omitted rather than guessed — the request says to keep the agent's own settings, and each optional parameter falls back to the agent when left out
No llm_integration / llm_connection_id is invented, and no API key appears anywhere in the YAML
The Slack task consumes the agent task's output through an OUTPUTS reference and depends on it, rather than set_outputs being set but never read

evals.prompt: Our 'Exec Dashboard Refresh' pipeline runs on a 6-field cron every 15 minutes and rebuilds the same aggregate tables each time, but a run sometimes takes 25 minutes and we're getting overlapping runs hammering the warehouse. Cap it to one run at a time, and make sure a trigger that lands while a run is in progress isn't just thrown away — we always want one more refresh after the current one, and only the freshest one. Write the pipeline YAML to pipeline.yml. Don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: A pipeline with configuration.concurrency.max_active: 1 and on_limit: QUEUE_LATEST — the refresh is idempotent and only the latest state matters, and on a 15-minute cron whose runs can take 25 minutes plain QUEUE would build an ever-growing backlog while the default SKIP would throw the trigger away, which the request rules out. Does not try to solve it by cancelling the in-progress run, which Orchestra never does.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
configuration.concurrency.max_active is 1
configuration.concurrency.on_limit is QUEUE_LATEST — only the latest refresh matters, and on a cron whose runs outlast the interval QUEUE would build an unbounded backlog
on_limit is set explicitly rather than left to the default, since the default SKIP would discard the trigger the request says to keep
Does not claim or configure cancellation of the in-progress run to free the slot — Orchestra never cancels in-progress runs to honour a concurrency limit
Does not invent a concurrency field outside configuration.concurrency (no top-level concurrency:, no max_active on a task)

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Partner Refresh' with a single Snowflake task running the stored procedure CALL analytics.refresh_partners(), on a cron trigger daily at 5am UTC. It goes in our Git-backed pipelines repo, and I'll be committing it on a branch called feat/partner-refresh. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml, and tell me what still has to happen before it starts running on schedule.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a SNOWFLAKE task running the stored procedure on a 5am daily cron, written to pipeline.yml. The handoff then says the committed file does not run on schedule from feat/partner-refresh: for a Git-backed pipeline the change only takes effect once it is merged into the pipeline's default branch, which is what Orchestra syncs from. May add that a run triggered against the branch uses the branch's version of the file if they want to try it before the merge, and should still call out the Snowflake connection or any UI setup needed.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the SNOWFLAKE integration for the stored procedure task
Scheduled daily at 5am UTC
The handoff states that the pipeline does not run on schedule until the change is merged into the pipeline's default branch, which is the branch Orchestra syncs the definition from
Does not claim that committing or pushing to feat/partner-refresh deploys the pipeline, and does not offer update_pipeline as a way to deploy a Git-backed pipeline

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline 'Finance Nightly' with a single dbt Core task running `dbt build`, on a cron trigger at 2am UTC daily. Our pipelines repo isn't on github.com — it lives on our GitHub Enterprise tenant at https://acme.ghe.com. Write it to pipeline.yml and tell me whether we can run this Git-backed at all, and what setup that needs.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a DBT_CORE / DBT_CORE_EXECUTE task running `dbt build` on a 2am daily cron, written to pipeline.yml. The handoff confirms a GHE.com tenant IS a supported home for Git-backed pipelines (GitHub Enterprise Cloud is a supported provider), and names what its setup needs: a GitHub App owned by their own organisation on the tenant, created during the workspace connection, so an owner of that GitHub organisation has to run it — and Orchestra's IPs added to the allow list first if the tenant or enterprise IP-restricts access. Should not confuse this with GitHub Enterprise Server, which is not supported.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the DBT_CORE integration for the dbt build task
Scheduled daily at 2am UTC
States that a repository on a GHE.com tenant is supported for Git-backed pipelines, because GitHub Enterprise Cloud is one of the supported Git providers
Names the GHE.com setup requirement: the workspace connects through a GitHub App owned by the customer's own GitHub organisation on that tenant, so an owner of that organisation has to do the setup
Does not claim that Git-backed pipelines require github.com, and does not tell the user their only option is an Orchestra-stored pipeline or a mirror of the repo on github.com
Does not treat the GHE.com tenant as GitHub Enterprise Server; if GHES is mentioned at all it is identified as the unsupported one

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline 'Warehouse Nightly' with a single Python task that runs `scripts/load.py` from our repo acme/data-platform, on a cron trigger at 3am UTC daily. Write it to pipeline.yml. Our workspace is already connected to GitHub through Orchestra's Git control, and the repo is on github.com and inside that same organisation. Do I need to mint a personal access token for the Python connection, and what goes in its GitHub Enterprise URL field?
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a PYTHON / PYTHON_EXECUTE_SCRIPT task running scripts/load.py from Git (source: GIT) on a 3am daily cron, written to pipeline.yml. The handoff answers both questions: no PAT is needed, because the connection's authentication method offers the workspace's Git connection as well as a token and defaults to the Git connection, and this repo is inside the connected organisation; and the GitHub Enterprise URL field is left empty, both because the repo is on github.com and because it is left empty on the Git-connection path regardless. A token is named only as the fallback for a repo outside the connected organisation or a provider with no workspace Git connection.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the PYTHON integration for the script task
Runs the script from Git rather than inline
Scheduled daily at 3am UTC
States that no personal access token is needed, because the connection can authenticate with the workspace's Git connection instead of a token
Identifies the Git connection as the default authentication method, rather than presenting a token as the only or the expected route
Says the GitHub Enterprise URL field is left empty here, and does not invent a value for it
If a token is mentioned at all, it is scoped to the fallback case — a repo outside the connected organisation or App installation, or a provider with no workspace Git connection

evals.prompt: Add a task to pipeline.yml that emails our finance distribution list once the nightly load finishes. It should come from reports@acme.com (verified in SES), go to finance-leads@acme.com and cfo@acme.com, copy data-eng@acme.com, subject 'Nightly load complete', and the body should be the summary text our upstream Summarise task sets as an output. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with an AWS_SES / AWS_SES_SEND_EMAIL task whose `to` and `cc` are YAML arrays of address strings (not a single newline-separated string), `from_address: reports@acme.com`, and the plain-text body in `body_text` referencing the upstream task's output. One email goes to everyone across to/cc/bcc, so the task is not repeated or fanned out per recipient.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the AWS_SES integration
Uses the AWS_SES_SEND_EMAIL job
The plain-text body is set with `body_text`, not a `message` field
`to` is a YAML array of address strings holding both finance-leads@acme.com and cfo@acme.com -- not one string with the addresses separated by newlines or commas
`cc` is also a YAML array, with data-eng@acme.com as its own list entry
A single AWS_SES_SEND_EMAIL task covers all three recipients, rather than one task per address -- one run sends one email to everyone across to/cc/bcc
`from_address` is reports@acme.com, the verified identity, rather than a recipient address

evals.prompt: Our Lightdash 'Revenue Overview' dashboard keeps showing yesterday's numbers to everyone after the models reload. Add a task to pipeline.yml that runs after our dbt build and clears the cached results for that dashboard -- its URL is https://lightdash.acme.com/projects/9a1/dashboards/4c2f0b7e-5d31-4a7b-9d55-2f1c8e6a0b33/view. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a LIGHTDASH / LIGHTDASH_CLEAR_RESULTS_CACHE task depending on the dbt task, `scope: DASHBOARD`, and `content_uuid` set to the UUID taken from the dashboard URL. Not LIGHTDASH_REFRESH_DASHBOARD with `invalidate_cache`, which only bypasses the cache for that task's own queries rather than clearing it for every viewer.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the LIGHTDASH_CLEAR_RESULTS_CACHE job
Scope is DASHBOARD, since one dashboard was named rather than the whole project
`content_uuid` is the UUID from the dashboard URL
Does not solve this with LIGHTDASH_REFRESH_DASHBOARD plus `invalidate_cache`, which only skips the cache for that task's own queries instead of clearing it for every viewer
The clear-cache task depends on the dbt build, so the cache is cleared after the models have reloaded rather than before

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline called 'Revenue Daily' with a single dbt Core task running 'dbt build --select tag:revenue;', on a cron trigger daily at 6am UTC. It goes in our Git-backed pipelines repo. We want it grouped under the 'finance' folder on the pipelines page like the rest of the finance work -- write the pipeline to pipeline.yml and tell me how it ends up in that folder.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a DBT_CORE / DBT_CORE_EXECUTE task running the build command on a 6am daily cron, written to pipeline.yml. The handoff then says a Git-backed pipeline's folder is not set in Orchestra: it comes from the repository plus the directory holding the YAML file on the pipeline's default branch, so the file belongs under finance/ in the repo, and the folder only appears once that location lands on the default branch. Does not tell the user to add a folder field to the YAML, or to use Orchestra's Move action, which is disabled for Git-backed pipelines.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the DBT_CORE integration
Scheduled daily at 6am UTC
Does not invent a `folder` key in the pipeline YAML — folder is not a field in the pipeline schema
States that the folder comes from where the YAML file sits in the repository — the repository plus the file's directory — rather than from anything set in Orchestra or in the YAML
Tells the user to put or move the file under a `finance/` directory in the repo to get the pipeline into that folder
Says the folder only takes effect once the file's location lands on the pipeline's default branch, not on a feature branch
Does not suggest Orchestra's Move action, a folder picker, or the pipeline storage dialog's Folder field as the way to move this pipeline — those are for Orchestra-backed pipelines

evals.prompt: Add a pipeline-level failure alert to pipeline.yml that POSTs to our on-call service. We already have an Orchestra webhook connection called webhook_oncall whose base URL is https://hooks.acme.com/orchestra/alerts — that URL is the endpoint itself, there's no extra path to call. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a pipeline-level alert on FAILED whose destination is `integration: WEBHOOK` with `connection_id: webhook_oncall` and no `destination` field — the base URL is already the full endpoint, and `destination` is a path appended to it rather than a replacement for it, so pasting https://hooks.acme.com/orchestra/alerts into `destination` would post to the base URL twice over. May note that saving the connection does not call the endpoint, so delivery is only proven once a real alert fires.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
The alert fires on FAILED
The WEBHOOK destination sets connection_id (SLACK/EMAIL require destination; PAGER_DUTY/TEAMS/WEBHOOK/DATADOG require connection_id)

The connection's base URL (hooks.acme.com/orchestra/alerts) does not appear anywhere in the YAML — `destination` is a path appended to that base URL, so repeating the full URL there would post to the base URL twice over
The WEBHOOK destination omits `destination` entirely (or leaves it empty) rather than inventing a path such as `/alerts` or `/`, because the connection's base URL is already the endpoint to call
Does not treat `destination` as a full-URL field, and does not move the endpoint URL off the connection into the pipeline YAML

evals.prompt: After our dbt build finishes, trigger the GitLab CI/CD pipeline on the main branch of data-platform/etl/exporter so the export job runs. It needs ENVIRONMENT set to production, and the pipeline's .gitlab-ci.yml declares `retries` and `dry_run` under spec:inputs -- pass retries as 3 and dry_run as false. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a GITLAB / GITLAB_RUN_PIPELINE task depending on the dbt task, `project: data-platform/etl/exporter` and `ref: main`. ENVIRONMENT goes in `variables` as a string; retries and dry_run go in `inputs`, which keeps their JSON types (3 as a number, false as a boolean) rather than stringifying them -- Orchestra rejects non-string `variables` values when the pipeline is saved. Both parameters are quoted JSON strings, not nested YAML mappings. May note that `variables` needs the GitLab project's 'Minimum role to use pipeline variables' setting to allow the token's user, which new gitlab.com projects do not.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the GITLAB integration
Uses the GITLAB_RUN_PIPELINE job
`project` is the full project path given, not a guessed numeric ID
`ref` is the branch to run on
ENVIRONMENT=production is passed in `variables`, whose values must all be strings
retries and dry_run go in `inputs`, not in `variables` — they are declared under spec:inputs, and `inputs` is the only one of the two that preserves JSON types
Inside `inputs`, retries stays the number 3 and dry_run stays the boolean false, rather than being quoted into the strings "3" and "false"
`variables` and `inputs` are each a quoted JSON string, not a nested YAML mapping — both parameters are typed as string in the schema
Does not put a non-string value in `variables`, which Orchestra rejects when the pipeline is saved rather than at run time
The GitLab task depends on the dbt build, so the export is triggered after the models have loaded
Does not reach for an HTTP / HTTP_REQUEST task against GitLab's API, or a GitLab pipeline trigger token, instead of the GITLAB integration

evals.prompt: After the nightly dbt build succeeds, kick off our downstream `customer-exports` Orchestra pipeline (id 7c9a1f2e-4b3d-4a8e-9f10-2c5d6e7a8b90). It should run with run_date set to ${{ START_DATE }}, and take everything else -- region, warehouse_size and the rest -- from that pipeline's `eu-nightly` input set rather than us restating each one here. Write the pipeline to pipeline.yml. Just the YAML file, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with an ORCHESTRA / TRIGGER_PIPELINE task depending on the dbt build. `pipeline_id` is the target pipeline's UUID, `run_inputs` carries only run_date, and `input_set: eu-nightly` names the target pipeline's input set to fill every input run_inputs leaves out. Does not restate region or warehouse_size in run_inputs, and does not invent a separate task or HTTP call to apply the input set. May note that the target pipeline must be published, and that a name no input set on the target matches fails the child run as soon as it starts.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Uses the ORCHESTRA integration
Uses the TRIGGER_PIPELINE job
Sets pipeline_id to the target pipeline's UUID
Names the input set with the `input_set` parameter
`run_inputs` carries run_date only — region and warehouse_size are left to the input set rather than restated, since input_set fills every input run_inputs does not give
Does not model the input set as a run_inputs key, a pipeline-level `inputs` block, or a second task — `input_set` is a parameter of the TRIGGER_PIPELINE task itself
The TRIGGER_PIPELINE task depends on the dbt build, so the export pipeline starts after the models have loaded

evals.prompt: Create an Orchestra pipeline 'Orders Load' with one Snowflake query task running `CALL load_orders()`. It takes two inputs: `warehouse` (string, defaults to DEV_WH) and `full_refresh` (boolean, defaults to false). We run it three ways and don't want three copies of the pipeline: a nightly production run at 2am UTC on PROD_WH, a monthly backfill at 4am UTC on the 1st that also runs on PROD_WH but with full_refresh on, and ad-hoc dev runs that just take the defaults. Keep the per-run values on the pipeline so nobody has to retype them. Write it to pipeline.yml -- just the YAML, don't deploy it.
evals.expected_output: An Orchestra v1 pipeline YAML with a SNOWFLAKE / SNOWFLAKE_RUN_QUERY task, an `inputs:` block declaring `warehouse` and `full_refresh` with the given defaults, and a top-level `input_sets:` block holding the reusable values -- a `prod` set with `warehouse: PROD_WH` and a backfill set. Two `schedule:` entries name their set with `input_set:`; the backfill entry gets `full_refresh: true` either from its own set or from that entry's `run_inputs`. Ad-hoc runs name no set and fall through to the declared defaults. The sets are not presented as environments and no environment is expected to select one.

assertions.text: Output is a valid YAML document
Pipeline declares version v1
Declares a top-level `input_sets:` block rather than duplicating the pipeline or hardcoding the values on each schedule
At least one schedule entry names a set with `input_set:`
The production warehouse value is held in a set rather than repeated on each trigger
`input_sets:` sits at the pipeline's top level, a sibling of `inputs:` and `schedule:`, not nested inside `inputs:` or inside a schedule entry
Every key used inside an input set is one of the pipeline's declared inputs (`warehouse`, `full_refresh`) -- a set cannot introduce an input that `inputs:` does not declare
Each input set is partial: it sets only the inputs it changes and leaves the rest to their declared `default`, rather than restating every input in every set

The backfill run gets `full_refresh: true` from its own input set or from that schedule entry's `run_inputs`, and does not change the `full_refresh` default to true (which would affect ad-hoc dev runs too)

Does not conflate input sets with environments: no claim that running in a production environment applies a `prod` input set, and the sets are not offered as a replacement for environment variables or connections
Ad-hoc dev runs are left to name no input set and take the declared defaults, rather than being given a `dev` set that merely restates those defaults
